flashcards.q: Why is a GCP VPC described as a global resource, and what changes as a result?
flashcards.a: A VPC's subnets are regional, but the VPC itself spans every region with no cross-region peering or transit gateway needed -- two subnets in different regions in the same VPC are reachable over Google's backbone by default. AWS/Azure networks are strictly regional and always need explicit cross-region plumbing.

flashcards.q: What is the default scope of a GCP firewall rule, and what's the common mistake it causes?
flashcards.a: VPC-scoped (global) by default -- applies to every matching instance in every region of the VPC unless explicitly scoped with target tags or service accounts. AWS engineers used to regionally-scoped security groups often assume implicit regional scoping that doesn't exist, creating unintentionally broad rules.

flashcards.q: How does Shared VPC work and what IAM role does a service project need?
flashcards.a: A host project owns the VPC, subnets, routes, and firewall rules; service projects attach and deploy resources INTO the host's subnets without owning networking resources. Requires roles/compute.networkUser granted per subnet (preferred) or project-wide on the host.

flashcards.q: How does GCP's global external Application Load Balancer route traffic, mechanically?
flashcards.a: A single global anycast IP is announced from every Google PoP simultaneously (BGP anycast). User traffic enters at the nearest PoP, travels Google's private backbone (Premium Tier), and reaches the nearest healthy backend in any region -- automatic geo-routing and instant health-check failover with no DNS TTL dependency.

flashcards.q: When should you choose a regional load balancer over the global anycast LB?
flashcards.a: Data-residency requirements, active-passive DR needing explicit regional control, genuinely single-region traffic where global's cost premium buys nothing, or Standard Tier (internet-routed, cheaper) networking instead of Premium Tier backbone routing.

flashcards.q: What are Cloud Armor's two pricing tiers and what does Enterprise add?
flashcards.a: Standard: pay-as-you-go, ~$1/rule/month, basic WAF/DDoS rules + rate limiting. Enterprise: ~$3,000/month, adds Adaptive Protection (ML-based anomaly detection tuned to backend traffic baseline) and DDoS bill protection (credits for attack-driven cost spikes).

flashcards.q: Why do static per-IP rate limits fail against a real botnet attack, and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: A distributed botnet uses thousands of rotating source IPs, so no single IP crosses the per-IP threshold even though aggregate backend load is severe. Fix: Adaptive Protection (Enterprise tier) does ML-based anomaly detection against the backend's aggregate traffic pattern rather than relying on any single per-IP dimension.

flashcards.q: What does Private Service Connect give you that VPC peering doesn't?
flashcards.a: Private IP access to a published service inside the consumer's own VPC without peering the two networks -- no IP-overlap coordination needed, no broad transitive-reachability exposure, and the producer controls exactly which consumers can connect via accept lists on the service attachment.

flashcards.q: Compare Dedicated, Partner, and Cross-Cloud Interconnect.
flashcards.a: Dedicated: direct physical circuit into Google colocation, 10Gbps/100Gbps ports, VLAN attachments 50Mbps-50Gbps, needs own colocation presence. Partner: via a supported service provider, sub-10Gbps, no colocation needed, faster provisioning, higher per-GiB egress at scale. Cross-Cloud Interconnect: direct Google-provisioned link straight to AWS/Azure, no third-party colocation partner.

flashcards.q: When do you use VPC Network Peering instead of Shared VPC?
flashcards.a: Peering connects two genuinely SEPARATE VPCs (different Shared VPC hosts, different orgs, M&A integration). Shared VPC is for one network with delegated usage rights across multiple teams/projects within the same org -- not a default multi-region pattern, since GCP's global VPC already gives cross-region reachability without either.

flashcards.q: What's the incomplete part of claiming 'Cloud Armor is just AWS WAF renamed'?
flashcards.a: Both provide comparable L7 WAF rules and rate limiting, but Cloud Armor sits in front of GCP's global anycast LB, so volumetric attacks are structurally absorbed/distributed across Google's entire edge before rules even fire. AWS WAF on a bare regional ALB doesn't get that dilution unless separately paired with CloudFront or Global Accelerator.

flashcards.q: What operationally changes migrating a two-region AWS Transit-Gateway topology to GCP?
flashcards.a: Transit Gateway's routing/attachment machinery mostly disappears -- same-org resources become subnets of one GCP VPC with default reachability. What replaces centralized routing control is disciplined firewall-rule scoping (default permissive-within-VPC) and Shared VPC with per-subnet IAM grants for team isolation. The model inverts: AWS = explicit reachability/implicit isolation; GCP = implicit reachability/explicit isolation.
